blocks.html: Real analysis is the part of mathematics that proves why calculus works. Almost every proof in it measures how close two numbers are, and the tool for that is the absolute value. You solved inequalities like $|x - 3| < 2$ in Algebra 1, and in Discrete Math you learned to write a direct proof. This course puts the two together.

$|x - a|$ is the distance from $x$ to $a$, so $|x - a| < \varepsilon$ means $a - \varepsilon < x < a + \varepsilon$. Two inequalities turn distances into bounds: the triangle inequality $|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$, and the reverse triangle inequality $|a| - |b| \le |a - b|$.

Since $-|a| \le a \le |a|$ and $-|b| \le b \le |b|$, adding gives $-(|a| + |b|) \le a + b \le |a| + |b|$, which says exactly $|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$. For the reverse version, write $a = (a - b) + b$ and apply the triangle inequality: $|a| \le |a - b| + |b|$, so $|a| - |b| \le |a - b|$. Swapping $a$ and $b$ gives $|b| - |a| \le |a - b|$ too, so in fact $\big||a| - |b|\big| \le |a - b|$.

Analysts use these two facts in two directions. The triangle inequality gives an upper bound for a sum: if two quantities are each small, so is their sum. The reverse inequality gives a lower bound: a number close to $a$ cannot be much smaller in size than $|a|$. We will use the second one to keep denominators away from $0$.

blocks.title: Unwrapping an absolute value
blocks.q: Write the set of $x$ with $|x + 2| < 0.1$ as an interval.
blocks.a: $(-2.1, -1.9)$, an open interval because the inequality is strict.

blocks.title: Bounding a factor
blocks.q: If $|x - 3| < 1$, how big can $|x + 3|$ be?
steps: This is the step that makes $x^{2}$ continuous at $3$: $|x^{2} - 9| = |x - 3|\,|x + 3| < 7|x - 3|$, which is small when $|x - 3|$ is.
blocks.a: $|x + 3| < 7$, and no smaller bound works for every such $x$.

blocks.title: Keeping away from zero
blocks.q: If $|x - 5| < 2$, show that $|x| > 3$.
blocks.a: $|x| > 3$. (So $\frac{1}{|x|} < \frac{1}{3}$: a bound on a reciprocal, the kind the quotient law needs.)

blocks.html: Running the inequality backward. The tempting "$|a - b| \le |a| - |b|$" is false: with $a = 1$ and $b = 2$, the left side is $1$ and the right side is $-1$. The difference of sizes is a lower bound for the size of the difference. And $|a + b| = |a| + |b|$ holds only when $a$ and $b$ have the same sign (or one is $0$). Check any inequality like these with $a = 1$, $b = -1$ and with $a = 1$, $b = 2$ before you use it.
In a proof you will often see a chain like $|x^{2} - 9| = |x - 3||x + 3| \le |x - 3|(|x - 3| + 6)$. The last step is the triangle inequality: $|x + 3| = |(x - 3) + 6| \le |x - 3| + 6$.

blocks.html: A bounded set of numbers may have no largest element. The set $(0, 1)$ has numbers as close to $1$ as you like, but $1$ itself is not in it. Analysis needs a name for the number such a set crowds up against, and in Discrete Math you met the set language we use to say it precisely. We also lean on distances throughout.

An upper bound of $A$ is a number $u$ with $a \le u$ for every $a \in A$. The supremum $\sup A$ is the least upper bound: it is an upper bound, and no smaller number is one. The infimum $\inf A$ is the greatest lower bound. When $\sup A$ belongs to $A$, it is the maximum; otherwise $A$ has no maximum.

Think of the upper bounds of $A$ as a ray on the number line, $[s, \infty)$. Its left end $s$ is the supremum. Every element of $A$ sits at or to the left of $s$ (so $s$ is an upper bound), and every number to the left of $s$ is beaten by some element (so nothing smaller is an upper bound). Whether $s$ itself is an element is a separate question, which is why "sup" and "max" are different words.

blocks.name: ra-supinf
blocks.cap: The set $\left\{1 - \frac{1}{n}\right\}$: the gold region holds the upper bounds; their left end is the supremum. Drag the red marker $b$ to test candidates.

blocks.title: A sequence that climbs
blocks.q: Find $\sup A$ and $\inf A$ for $A = \left\{1 - \frac{1}{n} : n \ge 1\right\}$.
steps: The elements are $0, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{3}{4}, \ldots$: increasing, and always less than $1$.
$\inf A = 0$, and it is an element (at $n = 1$), so it is the minimum.
Every element is below $1$, so $1$ is an upper bound. A smaller number $1 - \varepsilon$ is beaten as soon as $\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon$. So $\sup A = 1$, and $A$ has no maximum.

blocks.title: An interval with an extra point
blocks.q: Find $\sup A$ and $\inf A$ for $A = (-2, 1] \cup \{3\}$.
steps: The largest element is the isolated point $3$, so $\sup A = 3 = \max A$.
The elements come as close to $-2$ as you like, but $-2 \notin A$. So $\inf A = -2$, and there is no minimum.

blocks.title: Signs that alternate
blocks.q: Find $\sup A$ and $\inf A$ for $A = \left\{\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n} : n \ge 1\right\}$.
steps: The positive ones are largest at $n = 2$, and the negative ones are smallest at $n = 1$.

blocks.html: Sup is not max. Students often write "$\sup (0, 1)$ does not exist" or "$\sup A$ must be in $A$." The supremum exists for every nonempty set that is bounded above (that is the next topic), but it need not be an element. The opposite slip is giving an upper bound that is too big, like "$\sup (0, 1) = 2$." Check both conditions: is it an upper bound, and is every smaller number beaten by some element?

blocks.html: The definition of supremum has two halves, and proofs have to check both. The first half, "$s$ is an upper bound," is usually easy. The second half, "nothing smaller is an upper bound," has a convenient form called the ε-test, and it is the first place in this course where the letter $\varepsilon$ does real work.

Let $s$ be an upper bound of $A$. Then $s = \sup A$ exactly when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $a \in A$ with $a > s - \varepsilon$. In words: every number below $s$, however slightly below, is beaten by an element of $A$.

A number smaller than $s$ can always be written as $s - \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. "No number smaller than $s$ is an upper bound" says each $s - \varepsilon$ fails to be an upper bound, that is, some element exceeds it. That is word for word the ε-test. Conversely, if the test holds, every $s - \varepsilon$ is beaten, so no smaller upper bound exists.

Here is a full proof in this style. Claim: $\sup\left\{1 - \frac{1}{n} : n \ge 1\right\} = 1$. Proof. Every element is $1 - \frac{1}{n} < 1$, so $1$ is an upper bound. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. By the Archimedean property choose a positive integer $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon$. Then $1 - \frac{1}{n} > 1 - \varepsilon$, so $1 - \varepsilon$ is not an upper bound. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $1$ is the least upper bound. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: ra-supinf
blocks.cap: The ε-test: the blue strip is $(\sup - \varepsilon, \sup]$. However thin you make it with the slider, some term of the sequence (green) lands inside.

blocks.title: Which element passes the test?
blocks.q: For $A = \left\{1 - \frac{2}{n} : n \ge 1\right\}$ and $\varepsilon = 0.01$, find the smallest $n$ whose element is greater than $1 - \varepsilon$.
steps: The smallest whole number with $n > 200$ is $201$.

blocks.title: An element of an interval
blocks.q: For $A = [2, 5)$ and $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{4}$, give an element greater than $5 - \varepsilon$.

blocks.title: The same test for an infimum
blocks.q: Show that $\inf A = 2$ for $A = \left\{2 + \frac{3}{n} : n \ge 1\right\}$, and find the first element below $2 + 0.01$.
steps: Every element is $2 + \frac{3}{n} > 2$, so $2$ is a lower bound.

For the ε-test turned around, we need an element below $2 + \varepsilon$: $\frac{3}{n} < \varepsilon$ holds once $n > \frac{3}{\varepsilon}$, which the Archimedean property supplies. So $2$ is the greatest lower bound.
With $\varepsilon = 0.01$: $n > 300$, so the first such element is at $n = 301$.
blocks.a: $\inf A = 2$; the first element below $2.01$ is $2 + \frac{3}{301}$, at $n = 301$.

blocks.html: Proving only half. "Every $x$ in $(0, 2)$ has $x < 2$, so $\sup (0, 2) = 2$" proves only that $2$ is an upper bound, which gives $\sup (0, 2) \le 2$. The number $3$ is an upper bound too. To pin down the supremum you must also show every smaller number fails. A second slip is checking the test for one $\varepsilon$, like $0.01$: the test must hold for every $\varepsilon > 0$, so the proof starts "Let $\varepsilon > 0$" and then works for that arbitrary $\varepsilon$.

blocks.html: The rational numbers have every algebraic property the reals have, so what makes $\mathbb{R}$ special? In Algebra 1 the answer was "the reals fill in the gaps, like $\sqrt{2}$." Analysis makes that precise with one axiom about suprema.

Completeness axiom. Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum in $\mathbb{R}$. Archimedean property (a consequence): for every real $x$ there is a positive integer $n > x$; equivalently, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a positive integer $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon$.

Suppose the positive integers were bounded above. By completeness they would have a supremum $s$. Then $s - 1$ is not an upper bound, so some integer $n$ has $n > s - 1$. But then $n + 1 > s$, and $n + 1$ is a positive integer, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. So for every $x$ some integer exceeds it. Taking $x = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ gives $n > \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, that is, $\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon$.

Completeness is exactly what fails in $\mathbb{Q}$. The set $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x > 0,\ x^{2} < 2\}$ is bounded above (by $2$, say), and in $\mathbb{R}$ its supremum is $\sqrt{2}$. But $\sqrt{2}$ is not rational, and no rational number can serve as the least upper bound: any rational upper bound $r$ has $r^{2} > 2$, and a slightly smaller rational is still an upper bound. Every limit theorem in this course (monotone sequences converge, the intermediate value theorem, the extreme value theorem) uses completeness somewhere, and each one is false in $\mathbb{Q}$.

blocks.name: ra-supinf
blocks.cap: Rationals with $x^{2} < 2$ crowd up against $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$. The supremum exists in $\mathbb{R}$, not in $\mathbb{Q}$.

blocks.title: The Archimedean property with numbers
blocks.q: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} < 0.003$.
steps: The smallest whole number above $333.\overline{3}$ is $334$.

blocks.title: When equality is close
blocks.q: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{30}$.
steps: $n = 30$ gives equality, which is not "less than."

blocks.title: A supremum outside the set's number system
blocks.q: Let $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x > 0,\ x^{2} < 5\}$. What is $\sup S$, and is it rational?
steps: Every element is less than $\sqrt{5}$, and rationals come arbitrarily close to $\sqrt{5}$ (density, next topic).
So $\sup S = \sqrt{5}$, which is irrational because $5$ is not a perfect square.

blocks.html: Assuming suprema stay in the same number system. A bounded set of rationals need not have a rational supremum, as $S$ above shows. In a proof, "let $s = \sup A$" is allowed only when $A$ is a nonempty set of reals bounded above, and then $s$ is a real number. Check both hypotheses (nonempty, bounded above) every time you invoke completeness.

blocks.html: Between any two different real numbers there are infinitely many rationals, even though the rationals have "gaps." The proof is a short, concrete recipe built on the Archimedean property, and it is a model for many analysis proofs: choose a scale, then count steps.

Density of $\mathbb{Q}$. If $a < b$, there is a rational $\frac{m}{n}$ with $a < \frac{m}{n} < b$. Recipe: choose a positive integer $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} < b - a$; then let $m$ be the smallest integer greater than $na$.

Steps of size $\frac{1}{n}$ are shorter than the gap $b - a$, so they cannot jump over the whole interval $(a, b)$. Precisely: $m$ is the smallest integer with $m > na$, so $m - 1 \le na$. Dividing by $n$: $a < \frac{m}{n}$ and $\frac{m}{n} \le a + \frac{1}{n} < a + (b - a) = b$. So $\frac{m}{n}$ is strictly between $a$ and $b$. The integer $m$ exists because the integers have no gaps: $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$.

Applying the result again to $\left(a, \frac{m}{n}\right)$ gives another rational, and so on: there are infinitely many. The same idea shows the irrationals are dense too: find a rational $q$ between $\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}$ with $q \ne 0$; then $q\sqrt{2}$ is irrational and lies between $a$ and $b$.

blocks.title: Following the recipe
blocks.q: Find a fraction between $a = 0.31$ and $b = 0.34$ using the recipe.
steps: $na = 34 \cdot 0.31 = 10.54$, so the smallest integer above it is $m = 11$.

blocks.title: Next to an irrational
blocks.q: Use the recipe for $a = \sqrt{2}$ and $b = 1.42$.

blocks.html: Choosing $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} \le b - a$, or $m$ with $m \ge na$. With equality allowed, the fraction can land exactly on $b$ (or on $a$). For $a = 0$ and $b = \frac{1}{2}$, the choice $n = 2$ gives $\frac{1}{n} = b - a$ and $m = 1$, so $\frac{m}{n} = \frac{1}{2} = b$, not strictly inside. The strict inequalities in the recipe are what make the final check $a < \frac{m}{n} < b$ work.

The recipe is not the only route. The fraction with the smallest denominator between $0.31$ and $0.34$ is $\frac{1}{3}$; the proof only needs some fraction, and it chooses one that is easy to justify.

blocks.html: Some infinite sets are bigger than others. In Discrete Math you saw that a bijection matches two sets element for element; here we compare infinite sets the same way. The surprise, due to Georg Cantor, is that the real numbers cannot be listed at all, even though the rationals can. The proof uses decimal expansions of numbers in $(0, 1)$, which exist thanks to completeness.

A set is countable when it is finite or there is a bijection between it and the positive integers, that is, its elements can be listed $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ with every element appearing. $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ are countable. The interval $(0, 1)$, and so $\mathbb{R}$, is uncountable.

Pairs are countable. List the pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers by diagonals $m + n = 2, 3, 4, \ldots$: $(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1), \ldots$ Each diagonal is finite, so every pair gets a position, and $\frac{m}{n}$ then lists every positive rational (with repeats, which we skip). $(0, 1)$ is not. Suppose $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$ were a list of all of $(0, 1)$. Build $x = 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots$ where $d_k = 4$ if the $k$th digit of $x_k$ is $5$, and $d_k = 5$ otherwise. Then $x \in (0, 1)$, and $x$ differs from $x_k$ in the $k$th digit, so $x \ne x_k$ for every $k$. Using only the digits $4$ and $5$ means $x$ has a unique decimal expansion (no $\ldots 999$ tail), so "differs in a digit" really means "is a different number." So the list missed $x$: no list can contain all of $(0, 1)$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: ra-diagonal
blocks.cap: Build the diagonal number one digit at a time. Each new digit is chosen to disagree with the digit on the diagonal.

blocks.name: ra-diagonal
blocks.cap: The diagonal listing of pairs: step through it and watch every pair receive a position.

blocks.title: A position in the pair listing
blocks.q: In the diagonal listing, what is the position of $(3, 2)$?
steps: It lies on the diagonal $m + n = 5$.
The earlier diagonals $m + n = 2, 3, 4$ hold $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ pairs.
Within its diagonal it is number $m = 3$, so its position is $6 + 3 = 9$.

blocks.title: Building the diagonal number
blocks.q: A list begins $x_1 = 0.5172\ldots$, $x_2 = 0.3909\ldots$, $x_3 = 0.4455\ldots$, $x_4 = 0.8125\ldots$. Give the first four digits of Cantor's $x$.

blocks.html: "The diagonal number is just further down the list." It cannot be: if it were $x_{1000}$, then its $1000$th digit would have to equal the $1000$th digit of $x_{1000}$, but it was built to differ there. The argument does not search the list; it shows every single line fails. Another slip is thinking a list that "goes on forever" must eventually include everything. The integers $2, 4, 6, \ldots$ go on forever and still miss every odd number.

blocks.html: In Calculus 2 you said $a_n \to L$ when the terms "get closer and closer" to $L$. That phrase is not precise enough to prove anything: $1 + \frac{1}{n}$ gets closer and closer to $0$ as well, without ever getting close. The fix is a definition with two quantifiers, the kind you read in Discrete Math, and it rests on the Archimedean property.

$a_n \to L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $n \ge N$. The $\varepsilon$ is a challenge (how close?), and $N$ is the answer (from where on?). If one $N$ works, every larger $N$ works too.

Read the definition as a game. A skeptic names a tolerance $\varepsilon$, as tiny as they like. You must answer with a point $N$ in the sequence beyond which every term stays within $\varepsilon$ of $L$, not just one term, and not just most of them. A sequence converges to $L$ when you can always win, whatever $\varepsilon$ the skeptic picks. For $1 + \frac{1}{n}$ and $L = 0$ the skeptic wins with $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}$: every term is more than $1$ away from $0$.

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: Terms of $a_n = \frac{2n + 1}{n + 3}$ with the band $L \pm \varepsilon$ around $L = 2$. Drag $N$ (or use the arrow keys): terms from $N$ on turn green inside the band and red outside. Shrink $\varepsilon$ and watch the smallest working $N$ grow.

blocks.title: Finding $N$ for one $\varepsilon$
blocks.q: Let $a_n = \frac{2n + 1}{n + 3}$, so $L = 2$. Find an $N$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.01$.
steps: Since $\frac{5}{n + 3}$ decreases, every $n \ge 498$ works, and $n = 497$ gives exactly $0.01$, which is not less than $0.01$.

blocks.title: Checking a proposed $N$
blocks.q: For $a_n = \frac{1}{n^{2}}$ ($L = 0$) and $\varepsilon = 0.001$, does $N = 30$ work?
steps: At $n = 30$ the distance is $\frac{1}{900} \approx 0.0011$, which is not below $0.001$.
blocks.a: No. The smallest $N$ that works is $32$.

blocks.title: A sequence that zigzags
blocks.q: Let $a_n = \frac{3 + 2(-1)^{n}}{n}$, with limit $0$. Find the smallest $N$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.1$.
steps: For even $n$, $|a_n| = \frac{5}{n}$; for odd $n$, $|a_n| = \frac{1}{n}$. The distances are not monotone.
Even $n$: need $\frac{5}{n} < 0.1$, so $n > 50$; the last even failure is $n = 50$. Odd $n$: $\frac{1}{n} < 0.1$ once $n > 10$; the last odd failure is $n = 9$.
The last failing index is $50$, so every $n \ge 51$ works.

blocks.html: Checking one term instead of all the later ones. In the zigzag example, $|a_{11}| = \frac{1}{11} < 0.1$, but $N = 11$ fails because $a_{12}, a_{14}, \ldots$ are still too far. Always ask: does the inequality hold for every $n \ge N$? The opposite slip is thinking there is one correct $N$. If $N = 498$ works, so do $499$ and $10^{6}$; a definition that says "there is an $N$" never needs the smallest one.

blocks.html: Finding an $N$ for one $\varepsilon$, as in the definition, is a computation. A proof must handle every $\varepsilon > 0$ at once, so $N$ becomes a formula in $\varepsilon$. Every ε–N proof is written in two passes: scratch work backward, then a clean argument forward.

Scratch work (not part of the proof): simplify $|a_n - L|$, bound it by something simple like $\frac{C}{n}$, and solve $\frac{C}{n} < \varepsilon$ to see that $N > \frac{C}{\varepsilon}$ will do. The proof: "Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose an integer $N > \frac{C}{\varepsilon}$. Let $n \ge N$. Then $|a_n - L| \le \frac{C}{n} \le \frac{C}{N} < \varepsilon$."

The order of the sentences follows the order of the quantifiers in the definition: for every $\varepsilon$ (let $\varepsilon > 0$), there is an $N$ (choose it, using only $\varepsilon$), such that for all $n \ge N$ (let $n \ge N$), the inequality holds (the estimate). The scratch work runs the other way, starting from the inequality we want, which is why it cannot be handed in as a proof: it assumes what it is trying to show. Replacing $|a_n - L|$ by a simpler upper bound is allowed and makes the algebra easy; the bound only has to be true and to go to $0$.

Model proof. Claim: $\frac{3n + 1}{n + 2} \to 3$. Scratch: $\left|\frac{3n + 1}{n + 2} - 3\right| = \frac{5}{n + 2} < \frac{5}{n}$, and $\frac{5}{n} < \varepsilon$ when $n > \frac{5}{\varepsilon}$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. By the Archimedean property choose an integer $N > \frac{5}{\varepsilon}$. For every $n \ge N$, $\left|\frac{3n + 1}{n + 2} - 3\right| = \frac{5}{n + 2} < \frac{5}{n} \le \frac{5}{N} < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: The proof's choice $N > \frac{5}{\varepsilon}$ for $\frac{3n + 1}{n + 2} \to 3$: try several $\varepsilon$ and check that $N = \frac{5}{\varepsilon}$ (rounded up) always lands in the green.

blocks.title: Simplify, then bound
blocks.q: For $a_n = \frac{2n - 7}{n + 4}$ and $L = 2$, find a constant $C$ with $|a_n - L| < \frac{C}{n}$, and write the choice of $N$.
steps: Dropping the $4$ makes the denominator smaller and the fraction bigger: $\frac{15}{n + 4} < \frac{15}{n}$. So $C = 15$.

blocks.title: A bound that needs care
blocks.q: For $a_n = \frac{n}{n^{2} + 1}$ and $L = 0$, find a simple bound and the choice of $N$.

blocks.html: Handing in the scratch work. "Suppose $\frac{5}{n + 2} < \varepsilon$; then $n > \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 2$, so the limit is $3$" starts from the conclusion. Another common slip is an $N$ that depends on $n$ (like "choose $N = n + 1$"): $N$ must be fixed before $n$ is chosen, from $\varepsilon$ alone. And a proof that picks $\varepsilon = 0.01$ proves the inequality for that one $\varepsilon$, not convergence.

blocks.html: Two facts about convergence come straight from the definition: a convergent sequence cannot wander off to infinity, and a sequence can fail to converge in a precise way that you can exhibit with a single $\varepsilon$.

Convergent sequences are bounded: if $a_n \to L$, some $M$ has $|a_n| \le M$ for every $n$. Not converging to $L$ means: there is an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $N$ some $n \ge N$ has $|a_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.

Bounded. Use the definition with $\varepsilon = 1$: there is an $N$ with $|a_n - L| < 1$ for $n \ge N$, so those terms have $|a_n| < |L| + 1$ (triangle inequality). Only finitely many terms come before $N$. So $M = \max\{|a_1|, \ldots, |a_{N-1}|, |L| + 1\}$ bounds every term. $\blacksquare$ Negation. "For every $\varepsilon$ there is an $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$" becomes, one quantifier at a time: there is an $\varepsilon$ such that for every $N$ there is an $n \ge N$ with $|a_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: $a_n = (-1)^{n}$ with a band around $L = 0.5$: whatever $N$ you choose, some later term is outside the band when $\varepsilon \le 1.5$.

blocks.title: The bound from the proof
blocks.q: For $a_n = \frac{5n + 9}{n + 1}$, which tends to $5$, carry out the proof's recipe: find $N$ for $\varepsilon = 1$ and then $M$.
steps: $|a_n - 5| = \frac{4}{n + 1} < 1$ once $n + 1 > 4$, so the smallest $N$ is $4$ ($|a_3 - 5| = 1$ exactly, which is not less than $1$).

blocks.title: Proving divergence with one $\varepsilon$
blocks.q: Show that $a_n = (-1)^{n}$ does not converge to $L = \frac{1}{2}$, and give the largest $\varepsilon$ that witnesses it.
steps: The terms are $-1$ and $1$, each infinitely often. Their distances from $\frac{1}{2}$ are $\frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.
Beyond any $N$ there is an odd $n$, where $|a_n - \frac{1}{2}| = \frac{3}{2}$.
So every $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon \le \frac{3}{2}$ witnesses the failure; $\frac{3}{2}$ is the largest.
blocks.a: $\varepsilon = \frac{3}{2}$ (or anything smaller and positive). Since $L$ was arbitrary in this style of argument, $(-1)^{n}$ diverges.

blocks.html: The contrapositive of "convergent implies bounded" is a quick test for divergence: an unbounded sequence diverges. So $\sqrt{n}$, $\ln n$ and $(-2)^{n}$ all diverge, with no $\varepsilon$ needed. A bounded sequence needs a closer look.

Two traps. First, "bounded implies convergent" is false: $(-1)^{n}$ is bounded and diverges. Only the converse is true. Second, negating the definition as "for every $\varepsilon$, no $N$ works" says far too much: it would mean the sequence is never within any distance of $L$. The negation needs just one bad $\varepsilon$, and then for that $\varepsilon$ every $N$ fails somewhere later.

blocks.html: In Calculus 1 you used the limit laws freely. Now we prove them from the definition, which shows how ε-proofs combine. You will need boundedness for the product.

If $a_n \to a$ and $b_n \to b$, then $a_n + b_n \to a + b$, $c\,a_n \to ca$, $a_n b_n \to ab$, and $\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to \frac{a}{b}$ when $b \ne 0$. The proofs split $\varepsilon$ between the pieces ("$\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ each") and use $N = \max(N_1, N_2)$ so that both estimates hold at once.

Sum. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $N_1$ with $|a_n - a| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ for $n \ge N_1$, and $N_2$ with $|b_n - b| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ for $n \ge N_2$. For $n \ge N = \max(N_1, N_2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|(a_n + b_n) - (a + b)| \le |a_n - a| + |b_n - b| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$ Product. Add and subtract $a_n b$: $$a_n b_n - ab = a_n(b_n - b) + b(a_n - a).$$ Since $(a_n)$ converges it is bounded, say $|a_n| \le M$ with $M > 0$. Choose $N$ so that $|b_n - b| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2M}$ and $|a_n - a| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2|b| + 1}$ for $n \ge N$. Then $|a_n b_n - ab| < M\frac{\varepsilon}{2M} + |b|\frac{\varepsilon}{2|b| + 1} < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$ (The $+1$ avoids dividing by $0$ when $b = 0$.)

Quotient. It is enough to show $\frac{1}{b_n} \to \frac{1}{b}$, then use the product law. Since $b_n \to b \ne 0$, eventually $|b_n - b| < \frac{|b|}{2}$, and then $|b_n| > \frac{|b|}{2}$ by the reverse triangle inequality. So $\left|\frac{1}{b_n} - \frac{1}{b}\right| = \frac{|b - b_n|}{|b_n||b|} < \frac{2}{b^{2}}|b_n - b|$, which can be made smaller than any $\varepsilon$.

blocks.title: Splitting $\varepsilon$ with numbers
blocks.q: Suppose $|a_n - a| \le \frac{3}{n}$ and $|b_n - b| \le \frac{5}{n}$. For $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find $N_1$, $N_2$ and $N$ as in the sum proof.
steps: Each piece must be less than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2} = 0.05$.

blocks.title: Using the laws
blocks.q: If $a_n \to 3$ and $b_n \to -2$, find $\lim \frac{a_n b_n - a_n^{2}}{b_n + 4}$.
steps: The denominator tends to $2 \ne 0$, so the quotient law applies.

blocks.title: The step that protects a denominator
blocks.q: Suppose $b_n \to -4$. Explain why eventually $|b_n| > 2$, and bound $\left|\frac{1}{b_n} - \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)\right|$ in terms of $|b_n + 4|$.
steps: With $\varepsilon = 2 = \frac{|b|}{2}$ there is an $N$ with $|b_n + 4| < 2$ for $n \ge N$. By the reverse triangle inequality, $|b_n| \ge 4 - |b_n + 4| > 2$.

blocks.html: Using one $N$ for two sequences. "Choose $N$ so that $|a_n - a| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and $|b_n - b| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$" is fine only after saying why one $N$ serves both: take the larger of the two. In the product proof, the slip is forgetting to bound $|a_n|$: the factor $a_n$ changes with $n$, so "$|a_n||b_n - b|$ is small" needs $|a_n| \le M$ first.

blocks.html: Limits respect order, with one subtle exception. These facts, together with the limit laws, compute most limits without returning to $\varepsilon$ every time.

Order: if $a_n \le b_n$ for all $n$ (or all large $n$), $a_n \to a$ and $b_n \to b$, then $a \le b$. Squeeze: if $a_n \le c_n \le b_n$ for all large $n$ and $a_n \to L$ and $b_n \to L$, then $c_n \to L$. Strict inequalities can become equalities in the limit.

Order. Suppose instead $a > b$, and let $\varepsilon = \frac{a - b}{2}$. Eventually $a_n > a - \varepsilon$ and $b_n < b + \varepsilon$, and $a - \varepsilon = b + \varepsilon$, so $a_n > b_n$, a contradiction. Squeeze. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Eventually both $L - \varepsilon < a_n$ and $b_n < L + \varepsilon$, and then $L - \varepsilon < a_n \le c_n \le b_n < L + \varepsilon$, so $|c_n - L| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$

The squeeze theorem is how analysts handle anything bounded times something that goes to $0$: since $-1 \le \sin n \le 1$, $\left|\frac{\sin n}{n}\right| \le \frac{1}{n} \to 0$. It also handles sums of many small terms, by bounding every term by the smallest and the largest.

blocks.title: A bounded wiggle
blocks.q: Find $\lim \frac{3n + 2\sin n}{4n + 1}$.
steps: Divide top and bottom by $n$: $\frac{3 + 2\frac{\sin n}{n}}{4 + \frac{1}{n}}$.
$-\frac{1}{n} \le \frac{\sin n}{n} \le \frac{1}{n}$, so by the squeeze theorem $\frac{\sin n}{n} \to 0$.

blocks.title: A sum with $n$ terms
blocks.q: Find $\lim \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{n}{n^{2} + k}$.
steps: Each of the $n$ terms is between $\frac{n}{n^{2} + n}$ (the smallest, at $k = n$) and $\frac{n}{n^{2} + 1}$ (the largest, at $k = 1$).
So $\frac{n^{2}}{n^{2} + n} \le \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{n}{n^{2} + k} \le \frac{n^{2}}{n^{2} + 1}$, and both bounds tend to $1$.

blocks.title: A root of a sum
blocks.q: Find $\lim \left(2^{n} + 5^{n}\right)^{1/n}$.

blocks.title: Where a limit can land
blocks.q: Suppose $a_n \to L$ and $2 \le a_n \le 5$ for every $n \ge 10$. What can you say about $L$?
steps: Apply the order theorem to $2 \le a_n$ and to $a_n \le 5$ (the first nine terms do not matter).
So $2 \le L \le 5$. The ends are possible: $5 - \frac{1}{n} \to 5$ stays in $[2, 5]$.

blocks.html: Keeping a strict inequality in the limit. From $a_n < b_n$ you may conclude only $\lim a_n \le \lim b_n$. Example: $0 < \frac{1}{n}$ for every $n$, but both sides tend to $0$. In particular, a sequence of positive numbers can have limit $0$. Check any "$<$" in a limit argument against the example $\frac{1}{n}$.

blocks.html: Sometimes you cannot compute a sequence's terms in closed form, as with $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$. The monotone convergence theorem proves such a sequence converges without knowing the limit in advance, using completeness; after that, the limit laws find the limit. You met bounded monotone sequences in Calculus 2 as a fact; here is the proof.

Monotone convergence theorem. A bounded increasing sequence converges to $\sup\{a_n\}$; a bounded decreasing sequence converges to $\inf\{a_n\}$. For a recursion $a_{n+1} = g(a_n)$ with $g$ continuous: prove the sequence is monotone and bounded (usually by induction), and only then solve $L = g(L)$.

Let $(a_n)$ be increasing and bounded above, and let $s = \sup\{a_n\}$, which exists by completeness. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, the number $s - \varepsilon$ is not an upper bound, so some $a_N > s - \varepsilon$. Because the sequence increases, every $n \ge N$ has $s - \varepsilon < a_N \le a_n \le s$, so $|a_n - s| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$ The theorem says nothing about the value of $s$; the recursion supplies it, because $a_{n+1} \to s$ as well, so $s = g(s)$.

blocks.name: ra-cobweb
blocks.cap: Iterating $g(x) = \sqrt{2 + x}$ from $a_1 = 0$: up to the curve, across to the line $y = x$. The path climbs a staircase toward the crossing at $2$. Drag the start or press Step.

blocks.title: A nested square root
blocks.q: Let $a_1 = 0$ and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$. Show that $(a_n)$ converges and find its limit.
steps: Bounded: $a_1 < 2$, and if $a_n < 2$, then $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n} < \sqrt{4} = 2$. By induction, $a_n < 2$ for all $n$.
Increasing: for $0 \le x < 2$, $x^{2} < x + 2$ (since $x^{2} - x - 2 = (x - 2)(x + 1) < 0$), so $x < \sqrt{2 + x}$. Hence $a_n < a_{n+1}$.
So the sequence converges, to some $L$ with $0 \le L \le 2$. Then $L = \sqrt{2 + L}$, so $L^{2} - L - 2 = 0$ and $L = 2$ or $L = -1$. Since $L \ge 0$, $L = 2$.

blocks.title: A linear recursion
blocks.q: Let $a_1 = 0$ and $a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}a_n + 3$. Find $a_2$, $a_3$ and the limit.
steps: $a_2 = 3$, $a_3 = \frac{9}{2}$. The terms increase and stay below $6$ (if $a_n < 6$ then $a_{n+1} < 3 + 3 = 6$).

blocks.html: Solving $L = g(L)$ first. For $a_1 = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = 2a_n + 1$, the equation $L = 2L + 1$ gives $L = -1$, but the terms are $1, 3, 7, 15, \ldots$: there is no limit. The equation only says what a limit would have to be. Also, when the equation has two roots, use what you proved about the terms (all $\ge 0$, all below the smaller root, and so on) to choose the right one.

blocks.html: A subsequence keeps some of the terms of a sequence, in their original order. Subsequences are the main tool for showing that a sequence does not converge, and they lead to the most important existence theorem about sequences in the next topic. They build on limits of sequences.

A subsequence of $(a_n)$ is $(a_{n_k})$ where $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$ are positive integers. If $a_n \to L$, every subsequence tends to $L$. So if two subsequences have different limits, $(a_n)$ diverges. A subsequential limit is a number some subsequence converges to.

Strictly increasing indices satisfy $n_k \ge k$ (induction: $n_1 \ge 1$, and $n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k$). If $a_n \to L$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, take $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N$. For $k \ge N$ we have $n_k \ge k \ge N$, so $|a_{n_k} - L| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$ The proof uses the increasing indices in an essential way: they guarantee that the subsequence moves out along the sequence.

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: $a_n = (-1)^{n}\frac{2n}{n + 1}$, with the even terms highlighted in purple: they approach $2$, while the odd terms approach $-2$.

blocks.title: Two subsequences
blocks.q: Show that $a_n = (-1)^{n}\frac{2n}{n + 1}$ diverges.
blocks.a: Two subsequences with different limits, so $(a_n)$ diverges.

blocks.title: All subsequential limits
blocks.q: Find the set of subsequential limits of $a_n = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{3}\right)$.
steps: Each value occurs infinitely often, so each is the limit of a constant subsequence.
Any subsequence must eventually stay near one value (they are a fixed distance apart), so there are no others.

blocks.title: A subsequence along a pattern
blocks.q: Let $a_n = (-1)^{n}\frac{3n + 1}{n + 2}$. Find the limit of $a_{4k+3}$ as $k \to \infty$, and decide whether $a_{3k}$ converges.
steps: The index $4k + 3$ is always odd, so $a_{4k+3} = -\frac{3(4k + 3) + 1}{(4k + 3) + 2} \to -3$.
The index $3k$ is even for even $k$ and odd for odd $k$, so $a_{3k}$ itself has subsequences tending to $3$ and to $-3$: it diverges.

blocks.html: The set of subsequential limits tells a lot. A bounded sequence converges exactly when this set has one element. In the next topic you will see that it is never empty for a bounded sequence, and two topics later its largest and smallest elements get names: lim sup and lim inf.

Reordering is not a subsequence. $a_2, a_1, a_4, a_3, \ldots$ uses every term but in a different order, so it is not a subsequence, and the theorem says nothing about it. The indices must strictly increase: $n_k = k^{2}$ and $n_k = 2k + 1$ are fine; $n_k = \lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ (which repeats indices) is not. A second slip: one subsequence converging does not make the whole sequence converge.

blocks.html: A bounded sequence need not converge, but it cannot avoid having some convergent piece. This theorem is the engine behind the extreme value theorem, the convergence of Cauchy sequences, and compactness. Its proof combines subsequences with the monotone convergence theorem (through nested intervals).
Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem. Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.

Say every term lies in $I_0 = [a, b]$. Cut $I_0$ in half. At least one half contains $a_n$ for infinitely many $n$; call it $I_1$ (if both do, take the left one). Repeat: $I_2 \subseteq I_1$ is a half of $I_1$ holding infinitely many terms, and so on. The interval $I_k$ has length $\frac{b - a}{2^{k}}$. Now choose indices: $n_1$ with $a_{n_1} \in I_1$, then $n_2 > n_1$ with $a_{n_2} \in I_2$ (possible, since $I_2$ holds infinitely many terms), and so on. The left ends of the $I_k$ increase and are bounded, so they converge to some $c$ (monotone convergence), and the right ends converge to $c$ too, since the lengths go to $0$. Both $a_{n_k}$ and $c$ lie in $I_k$, so $|a_{n_k} - c| \le \frac{b - a}{2^{k}} \to 0$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: A bounded sequence with two piles: odd terms just above $\frac{1}{3}$, even terms just above $\frac{4}{5}$. The bisection keeps a half that holds infinitely many terms.

blocks.title: Running the bisection
blocks.q: Let $a_n = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{10n}$ for odd $n$ and $a_n = \frac{4}{5} + \frac{1}{10n}$ for even $n$, all in $[0, 1]$. Keeping the left half whenever it holds infinitely many terms, find $I_3$.
steps: The terms pile up at $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{4}{5}$ (from above). A closed half holds infinitely many terms exactly when one of these values lies in it.
$[0, \frac{1}{2}]$ contains $\frac{1}{3}$: keep it. Then $[0, \frac{1}{4}]$ does not contain $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{4}{5}$, so keep $[\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2}]$.

blocks.title: What the theorem promises
blocks.q: Does $(-1)^{n}$ converge? Does it have a convergent subsequence?
blocks.a: No; yes. The theorem promises a convergent subsequence, never convergence of the whole sequence.

blocks.html: Keeping the half with more of the early terms. What matters is a half with infinitely many terms; any finite number of terms can be ignored. In the example, the first terms of the sequence sit near $0.43$ and $0.85$, but where they are does not decide anything. Also, the theorem needs boundedness: $a_n = n$ has no convergent subsequence.

blocks.html: A divergent bounded sequence still has a largest and a smallest place where its terms pile up. These two numbers, the limit superior and limit inferior, always exist for bounded sequences (by Bolzano–Weierstrass and completeness), and they will power the root test and the radius of convergence later.

For bounded $(a_n)$, let $s_n = \sup\{a_k : k \ge n\}$ (the tail supremum) and $i_n = \inf\{a_k : k \ge n\}$. Then $\limsup a_n = \lim s_n$ and $\liminf a_n = \lim i_n$. They are the largest and the smallest subsequential limits, and $a_n$ converges exactly when $\limsup a_n = \liminf a_n$ (then both equal the limit).

As $n$ grows the tail $\{a_k : k \ge n\}$ loses elements, so its supremum can only go down: $(s_n)$ is decreasing, and it is bounded below. By monotone convergence it has a limit. The same works for $(i_n)$, which increases. Dropping finitely many terms never changes these limits, which is why they describe the long-run behavior and ignore early outliers. If $\limsup = \liminf = L$, then $i_n \le a_n \le s_n$ and both bounds tend to $L$, so $a_n \to L$ by the squeeze theorem.

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: $a_n = (-1)^{n}\left(1 + \frac{2}{n}\right)$: the red staircase is the tail suprema, falling to $\limsup a_n = 1$; the blue one is the tail infima, rising to $\liminf a_n = -1$.

blocks.title: Tails of an alternating sequence
blocks.q: For $a_n = (-1)^{n}\left(1 + \frac{2}{n}\right)$, find $\limsup a_n$, $\liminf a_n$, $\sup a_n$ and $s_5$.
steps: Even $n$: $1 + \frac{2}{n} \to 1$ from above. Odd $n$: $-1 - \frac{2}{n} \to -1$ from below.
The largest term overall is $a_2 = 2$, so $\sup a_n = 2$. From $k = 5$ on, the largest term is at the first even index, $k = 6$: $s_5 = 1 + \frac{2}{6} = \frac{4}{3}$.

blocks.title: A sequence that cycles
blocks.q: Find $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ of $a_n = (n \bmod 3) + \frac{1}{n}$.

blocks.html: For an unbounded sequence one writes $\limsup a_n = \infty$ when the terms are not bounded above. The examples in this course are bounded, so both numbers are finite.

Confusing $\sup$ with $\limsup$. The supremum of all the terms can be an early term that is never approached again, like $a_2 = 2$ above. The lim sup forgets any finite number of terms: it is where the tail suprema end up. Check by asking: do infinitely many terms come close to this value?

blocks.html: To use the definition of a limit you must already know the limit $L$. Cauchy's idea removes $L$: a sequence should converge when its terms get close to each other. In $\mathbb{R}$ that idea is exactly right, thanks to Bolzano–Weierstrass, and it is how we will handle series, whose sums are usually unknown.
$(a_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ with $|a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \ge N$. Theorem. A sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is Cauchy.

Convergent implies Cauchy: if $a_n \to L$, choose $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ for $n \ge N$; then $|a_m - a_n| \le |a_m - L| + |L - a_n| < \varepsilon$. Cauchy implies convergent: a Cauchy sequence is bounded (use $\varepsilon = 1$ as for convergent sequences). By Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence $a_{n_k} \to L$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, take $N$ from the Cauchy condition with $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$, and some $n_k \ge N$ with $|a_{n_k} - L| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$. For $n \ge N$: $|a_n - L| \le |a_n - a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} - L| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$ In $\mathbb{Q}$ the second half fails: the decimal truncations $1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \ldots$ of $\sqrt{2}$ are Cauchy, with no rational limit.

blocks.name: ra-epsband
blocks.cap: Cauchy mode for $a_n = \frac{3}{n}$: the shaded strip shows how far apart the terms from $N$ on can be. It must be narrower than $\varepsilon$.

blocks.title: Finding $N$ for a Cauchy sequence
blocks.q: For $a_n = \frac{3}{n}$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find the smallest $N$ with $|a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \ge N$.
steps: For $m, n \ge N$: $|a_m - a_n| = 3\left|\frac{1}{m} - \frac{1}{n}\right| < \frac{3}{N}$, and taking $m = N$ and $n$ huge comes as close to $\frac{3}{N}$ as you like.
So every pair is within $0.1$ exactly when $\frac{3}{N} \le 0.1$, that is, $N \ge 30$.

blocks.title: Neighbors close, but not Cauchy
blocks.q: Is $H_n = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}$ Cauchy?
steps: $H_{2n} - H_n = \frac{1}{n + 1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2n}$ has $n$ terms, each at least $\frac{1}{2n}$, so it is at least $\frac{1}{2}$.
blocks.a: No, so $H_n$ diverges, even though $H_{n+1} - H_n = \frac{1}{n + 1} \to 0$.

blocks.html: For a series $\sum a_k$, the difference of two partial sums is a block $a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_n$. So "the partial sums are Cauchy" says "far-out blocks are small," with no need to know the sum. That is the Cauchy criterion of the next unit.

Checking only consecutive terms. "$|a_{n+1} - a_n| \to 0$, so the sequence is Cauchy" is false: the harmonic sums above and $\sqrt{n}$ are counterexamples. The Cauchy condition is about every pair $m, n \ge N$, however far apart. Check with pairs like $(n, 2n)$ or $(n, 4n)$.

blocks.html: A series $\sum a_k$ is a sequence in disguise: its partial sums $s_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$. You met partial sums in Calculus 2. Since we rarely know the sum of a series in advance, the right tool is the Cauchy condition, which talks only about the terms.

$\sum a_k$ converges to $S$ when $s_n \to S$. Cauchy criterion: $\sum a_k$ converges if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ with $|a_{m+1} + a_{m+2} + \cdots + a_n| < \varepsilon$ whenever $n > m \ge N$. Taking $n = m + 1$ shows that a convergent series has $a_k \to 0$.

The block $a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_n$ is exactly $s_n - s_m$. So "far-out blocks are small" is the statement "the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence," which in $\mathbb{R}$ is the same as "the partial sums converge." The criterion is useful because blocks can often be estimated even when the sum is unknown, as in $\sum \frac{1}{k^{2}}$: comparing with the telescoping $\frac{1}{k - 1} - \frac{1}{k}$ gives $s_n - s_m < \frac{1}{m}$, which is small for large $m$. So $\sum \frac{1}{k^{2}}$ converges, and we never needed its sum ($\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}$).

The same criterion explains the classic divergence. For the harmonic series, the block $\frac{1}{n + 1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2n}$ has $n$ terms, each at least $\frac{1}{2n}$, so it is at least $\frac{1}{2}$ no matter how far out it starts. The criterion fails for $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}$, so the series diverges even though its terms go to $0$.

blocks.name: seriespartial
blocks.cap: Partial sums of $\sum \frac{1}{k^{2}}$ settle down; switch to the harmonic series to see sums that keep creeping up.

blocks.title: A telescoping series
blocks.q: Find $s_n$ and the sum for $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k(k + 1)}$, and the smallest $n$ with $S - s_n < 0.01$.

blocks.title: A geometric tail
blocks.q: For $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} = 1$, how many terms make the error less than $0.001$?
steps: The tail after $n$ terms is $\sum_{k > n} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$.

blocks.html: "The terms go to $0$, so the series converges." That is the most common series error. $a_k \to 0$ is necessary (it is the Cauchy criterion with blocks of one term), but not sufficient: $\sum \frac{1}{k}$ has terms going to $0$ and diverges, because long blocks do not get small. Use $a_k \to 0$ only to prove divergence: if the terms do not go to $0$, the series diverges.

blocks.html: Series with terms of both signs are harder: cancellation can help or hide what is going on. The Cauchy criterion gives a clean way to compare a series with a simpler one, and it proves the fact you used in Calculus 2 that absolutely convergent series converge.

Comparison test. If $|a_k| \le b_k$ for all $k$ and $\sum b_k$ converges, then $\sum a_k$ converges (absolutely). If $0 \le b_k \le a_k$ and $\sum b_k$ diverges, then $\sum a_k$ diverges. Absolute convergence: if $\sum |a_k|$ converges, then $\sum a_k$ converges. A series that converges but not absolutely converges conditionally.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\sum b_k$ converges, by the Cauchy criterion there is an $N$ with $b_{m+1} + \cdots + b_n < \varepsilon$ for $n > m \ge N$. By the triangle inequality, $$|a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_n| \le |a_{m+1}| + \cdots + |a_n| \le b_{m+1} + \cdots + b_n < \varepsilon.$$ So $\sum a_k$ satisfies the Cauchy criterion and converges. $\blacksquare$ Absolute convergence is the special case $b_k = |a_k|$. Notice what the proof needs: a convergent series above the absolute values. Being below a divergent series, or above a convergent one, gives nothing to work with.

In practice, finding the comparison series is the whole skill. Look at the terms for large $k$ and keep only the dominant parts: $\frac{k + 2}{k^{3} + 4}$ behaves like $\frac{k}{k^{3}} = \frac{1}{k^{2}}$, so compare with $\frac{C}{k^{2}}$. You do not need the best constant $C$, only one that works for all $k$ (or for all $k$ past some point, since finitely many terms never affect convergence). Bounded factors such as $\sin k$, $\cos k$ or $(-1)^{k}$ can be replaced by $1$ inside absolute values, which is why $\sum \frac{\sin k}{k^{2}}$ converges absolutely with no further work.

blocks.title: Comparing with a $p$-series
blocks.q: Show that $\sum \frac{k + 2}{k^{3} + 4}$ converges by finding the smallest $C$ with $\frac{k + 2}{k^{3} + 4} \le \frac{C}{k^{2}}$ for all $k \ge 1$.
steps: The values for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$ are $\frac{3}{5}$, $\frac{4}{3}$, $\frac{45}{31}$, $\frac{96}{68} = \frac{24}{17}$; after $k = 3$ the fraction $\frac{2k^{2} - 4}{k^{3} + 4}$ keeps shrinking.

blocks.title: Absolutely, conditionally, or not at all
blocks.q: Classify $\sum \frac{(-1)^{k}}{\sqrt{k}}$, $\sum \frac{\sin k}{k^{2}}$ and $\sum (-1)^{k}\frac{k}{k + 1}$.
steps: $\sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$ diverges ($p = \frac{1}{2}$), but the alternating series test gives convergence: conditional.
The terms do not go to $0$: divergent.

blocks.html: Comparing in the wrong direction. "$0 \le a_k \le \frac{1}{k}$ and $\sum \frac{1}{k}$ diverges, so $\sum a_k$ diverges" is invalid: $a_k = \frac{1}{k^{2}}$ satisfies the hypothesis and converges. Before using a comparison, say which way it points: smaller than convergent, or bigger than divergent (with nonnegative terms). Also, the comparison must use absolute values when $a_k$ can be negative.

blocks.html: For a decreasing sequence of positive terms, you can learn whether $\sum a_n$ converges by sampling it only at powers of $2$. This test is a neat application of comparison and settles the $p$-series without integrals.

Cauchy condensation test. If $a_n \ge 0$ and $(a_n)$ is decreasing, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ converges if and only if $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}$ converges. Moreover $\sum a_n \le \sum 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}$.

Group the terms in blocks of doubling length: $a_1$, then $a_2 + a_3$, then $a_4 + \cdots + a_7$, and so on; block $k$ is $a_{2^{k}} + \cdots + a_{2^{k+1} - 1}$, with $2^{k}$ terms. Because the terms decrease, each term of block $k$ is at most $a_{2^{k}}$ and at least $a_{2^{k+1}}$. So $$2^{k} a_{2^{k+1}} \le \text{block}_k \le 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}.$$ Summing the right inequality gives $\sum a_n \le \sum 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}$; summing the left one gives $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k \ge 1} 2^{k} a_{2^{k}} \le \sum a_n$. So the two series converge or diverge together. $\blacksquare$

For the $p$-series, $2^{k} a_{2^{k}} = 2^{k}(2^{k})^{-p} = (2^{1 - p})^{k}$, a geometric series with ratio $2^{1 - p}$. It converges exactly when $2^{1 - p} < 1$, that is, $p > 1$. For $a_n = \frac{1}{n(\ln n)^{p}}$, $2^{k} a_{2^{k}} = \frac{1}{(k \ln 2)^{p}}$, a constant times a $p$-series in $k$: it converges exactly when $p > 1$. So $\sum \frac{1}{n \ln n}$ diverges, extremely slowly.

Why does sampling at powers of $2$ help? A decreasing sequence changes slowly, so all the terms between $2^{k}$ and $2^{k+1}$ are about the same size as $a_{2^{k}}$; there are $2^{k}$ of them, so the block is about $2^{k}a_{2^{k}}$. Condensing turns a series whose terms shrink like a power of $n$ into one whose terms shrink geometrically, or not at all, and geometric behavior is easy to judge. It also explains logarithms: substituting $n = 2^{k}$ turns $\ln n$ into $k \ln 2$, so one layer of logarithm becomes a power of $k$.

blocks.title: The ratio of the condensed series
blocks.q: Apply condensation to $\sum \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}$.
blocks.a: Geometric with ratio $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, so the series converges.

blocks.title: A bound for a sum
blocks.q: Use $\sum a_n \le \sum_{k \ge 0} 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}$ to bound $\sum \frac{1}{n^{2}}$.

blocks.title: Logarithms in the denominator
blocks.q: Write the condensed term of $\sum_{n \ge 2} \frac{1}{n (\ln n)^{2}}$.
blocks.a: $\frac{1}{(\ln 2)^{2} k^{2}}$: a convergent $p$-series, so the original series converges.

blocks.html: Dropping the factor $2^{k}$, or ignoring "decreasing." The condensed series is $\sum 2^{k} a_{2^{k}}$, not $\sum a_{2^{k}}$; without the factor, $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ would seem to condense to the convergent $\sum \frac{1}{2^{k}}$. And the test needs decreasing terms: a sequence that is $0$ at the powers of $2$ and $\frac{1}{n}$ elsewhere has condensed series $0$ but diverges.

blocks.html: The ratio and root tests from Calculus 2 used ordinary limits. Many series have ratios or roots that jump around and have no limit. Replacing "lim" by lim sup fixes the root test completely, and the proof is a comparison with a geometric series, using absolute convergence.

Root test. Let $\rho = \limsup |a_k|^{1/k}$. If $\rho < 1$, $\sum a_k$ converges absolutely; if $\rho > 1$, it diverges. Ratio test. If $\limsup \left|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\right| < 1$, the series converges absolutely; if $\liminf \left|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\right| > 1$, it diverges. A value of exactly $1$ decides nothing.

Suppose $\rho < 1$ and pick $r$ with $\rho < r < 1$. Because the tail suprema of $|a_k|^{1/k}$ decrease to $\rho$, eventually $|a_k|^{1/k} < r$, that is, $|a_k| < r^{k}$ for all $k \ge K$. Comparing with the convergent geometric series $\sum r^{k}$ gives absolute convergence. If $\rho > 1$, then $|a_k|^{1/k} > 1$ for infinitely many $k$, so $|a_k| > 1$ infinitely often and $a_k \not\to 0$: divergence. $\blacksquare$ The root test is stronger than the ratio test: whenever the ratio test decides, the root test agrees, but not conversely.

Computing $\limsup |a_k|^{1/k}$ usually comes down to three facts: $k^{1/k} \to 1$ (so polynomial factors disappear), $c^{1/k} \to 1$ for any constant $c > 0$, and $(r^{k})^{1/k} = r$. For instance $\left(k^{5}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{k}\right)^{1/k} = \left(k^{1/k}\right)^{5}\cdot\frac{1}{3} \to \frac{1}{3}$, so $\sum k^{5}3^{-k}$ converges. When the terms follow different rules on different kinds of $k$, take the root of each kind; the lim sup is the largest of the limits you get.

blocks.title: Ratios that jump
blocks.q: Let $a_k = 2^{-k + (-1)^{k}}$. Compute the lim sup and lim inf of the ratios, and $\lim |a_k|^{1/k}$.
steps: So $\limsup$ of the ratios is $2$ and $\liminf$ is $\frac{1}{8}$: the ratio test cannot decide.
blocks.a: Ratios: $2$ and $\frac{1}{8}$; roots tend to $\frac{1}{2} < 1$, so the series converges.

blocks.title: Two geometric series interleaved
blocks.q: Let $a_k = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k}$ for even $k$ and $a_k = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{k}$ for odd $k$. Find $\limsup |a_k|^{1/k}$.

blocks.title: A limit that involves $e$
blocks.q: Find $\lim |a_k|^{1/k}$ for $a_k = \left(\frac{k}{k + 1}\right)^{k^{2}}$.

blocks.html: Using "lim" when it does not exist, or reading $1$ as divergence. In the first example the ratios have no limit, and a student who insists on $\lim \frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}$ gets stuck. Use lim sup. And when $\limsup |a_k|^{1/k} = 1$, both $\sum \frac{1}{k}$ (divergent) and $\sum \frac{1}{k^{2}}$ (convergent) are possible: switch tests.

The ratio test is easier to compute when the terms contain factorials, since $\frac{(k + 1)!}{k!} = k + 1$ cancels so neatly. The price is that it needs the ratios to behave; the root test needs nothing but the size of the terms. When the ratios do have a limit, the roots have the same limit, so the two tests then agree.

blocks.html: Alternating series converge for a very visual reason: the partial sums zigzag, and the zigzags shrink. You used the test in Calculus 2; here we prove it with nested intervals and the Cauchy criterion, and get a sharp error bound for free.

Alternating series test. If $b_k$ decreases and $b_k \to 0$, then $S = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} b_k$ converges, $S$ lies between any two consecutive partial sums, and $|S - s_n| < b_{n+1}$ (when $b_k$ strictly decreases).

The even partial sums increase: $s_{2m+2} = s_{2m} + (b_{2m+1} - b_{2m+2}) \ge s_{2m}$. The odd partial sums decrease: $s_{2m+1} = s_{2m-1} - (b_{2m} - b_{2m+1}) \le s_{2m-1}$. And every even sum is below every odd sum. So the even sums increase and are bounded above, hence converge, and the odd sums decrease to a limit too; their difference $s_{2m+1} - s_{2m} = b_{2m+1} \to 0$, so the limits agree. Call it $S$. Since $S$ sits between $s_n$ and $s_{n+1}$, its distance from $s_n$ is less than $|s_{n+1} - s_n| = b_{n+1}$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: seriespartial
blocks.cap: The alternating harmonic series on a number line: each step goes the other way and is shorter, so the sum is trapped between consecutive partial sums.

blocks.html: The error bound is one of the few in analysis that you get completely free: no derivatives to estimate, just the next term. It also tells you the sign of the error. If the last term you added was positive, you have overshot, and $s_n > S$; if it was negative, $s_n < S$. Averaging two consecutive partial sums is often much closer to $S$ than either one, because the true sum sits between them.

blocks.title: How many terms are enough?
blocks.q: How many terms of $\sum (-1)^{k+1}\frac{1}{k^{2}}$ guarantee an error below $0.001$?
steps: The error after $n$ terms is less than $b_{n+1} = \frac{1}{(n + 1)^{2}}$.

blocks.title: Above or below?
blocks.q: For $\sum (-1)^{k+1}\frac{1}{k}$, is $s_5$ above or below the sum?
steps: The fifth term is $+\frac{1}{5}$: adding it overshoots.
blocks.a: Above. Odd partial sums lie above $S$, even ones below.

blocks.title: Trapping the sum
blocks.q: Compute $s_3$ and $s_4$ for $\sum (-1)^{k+1}\frac{1}{k^{2}}$ and give the interval that must contain $S$.

blocks.html: The error bound uses the next term. After $n$ terms, the bound is $b_{n+1}$, the first term left out, not $b_n$. Also check the hypotheses: if $b_k$ is not decreasing (say $\frac{1}{k}$ for odd $k$ and $\frac{1}{k^{2}}$ for even $k$), the series can diverge even though $b_k \to 0$ and the signs alternate.

blocks.html: For finite sums, the order of the terms never matters. For series it can. Whether it does depends on the difference between absolute and conditional convergence, and the alternating harmonic series is the standard example.

If $\sum a_k$ converges absolutely, every rearrangement converges to the same sum. If $\sum a_k$ converges conditionally, then for every real number $T$ some rearrangement converges to $T$ (Riemann's rearrangement theorem), and others diverge.

Conditional case. Split the terms into positives and negatives. Both parts must diverge: if one converged, the other would equal the original series minus it and converge too, making the series absolutely convergent. So we have an unlimited supply of positive terms and of negative terms, each going to $0$. To reach $T$: add positive terms until the sum first exceeds $T$, then negative terms until it first drops below $T$, and repeat. Each overshoot is at most the last term used, and those terms go to $0$, so the partial sums converge to $T$. Absolute case. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $N$ with $\sum_{k > N} |a_k| < \varepsilon$. Far enough out, a rearrangement has used all of $a_1, \ldots, a_N$, and what remains is made of terms beyond $N$, whose total size is less than $\varepsilon$. So the rearranged sums end up within $\varepsilon$ of the original sum.

A famous case: taking two positive terms, then one negative, $1 + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{7} - \frac{1}{4} + \cdots$, gives $\frac{3}{2}\ln 2$ instead of $\ln 2$. In general, $p$ positive terms then $q$ negative terms give $\ln 2 + \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{p}{q}$.

blocks.name: seriespartial
blocks.cap: The alternating harmonic series in its original order settles at $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. A different order of the same terms settles somewhere else.

blocks.title: A rearranged partial sum
blocks.q: Find the sum of the first $6$ terms of $1 + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{7} - \frac{1}{4} + \cdots$.

blocks.title: Riemann's method for a target
blocks.q: To rearrange $1 - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} - \cdots$ toward $T = \frac{3}{2}$, how many positive terms come first?
steps: The sum first exceeds $1.5$ after three positive terms.
blocks.a: $3$; then negative terms are added until the sum drops below $1.5$ again.

blocks.html: Assuming addition is always commutative. Rearranging the terms of a conditionally convergent series can change its sum, or make it diverge. Before reordering or regrouping an infinite sum in a proof, check absolute convergence: for $\sum \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k^{2}}$ any order gives $\frac{\pi^{2}}{12}$, for $\sum \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}$ it does not.

blocks.html: You met the ε–δ definition of a limit in Calculus 1. It is the same idea as the ε–N definition, with "far enough out in the sequence" replaced by "close enough to $a$." This time we treat it as a working tool: given $\varepsilon$, find a $\delta$ and check it.

$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ (and $x$ is in the domain). If a $\delta$ works, so does every smaller positive $\delta$. The condition $0 < |x - a|$ means the value $f(a)$, if any, plays no role.

The $\varepsilon$ is a horizontal band around $L$; $\delta$ is a vertical window around $a$. The definition asks that the graph over the window (with the point $x = a$ removed) stays inside the band. Narrowing the window can only remove points, so it never breaks the condition, which is why any smaller $\delta$ works. The largest $\delta$ that works is set by the nearest place where the graph leaves the band.

blocks.name: ra-epsdelta
blocks.cap: The ε–δ box for $f(x) = x^{2}$ at $a = 2$. The part of the graph over the δ-window is green inside the ε-band and red where it escapes. Press "Largest δ," then shrink ε and watch δ shrink too.

blocks.title: A line
blocks.q: For $f(x) = 3x - 1$, $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$. Find the largest $\delta$ for $\varepsilon = 0.06$.

blocks.title: A removable hole
blocks.q: $f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 9}{x - 3}$ for $x \ne 3$. Find a $\delta$ for $\varepsilon = 0.01$ at $a = 3$, where the limit is $6$.
steps: This is less than $0.01$ exactly when $|x - 3| < 0.01$.
blocks.a: $\delta = 0.01$. The point $x = 3$ itself is excluded by $0 < |x - 3|$, which is lucky: $f(3)$ is undefined.

blocks.title: The square root, where the sides differ
blocks.q: For $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ at $a = 9$ (limit $3$) and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find the largest $\delta$.
steps: The distances from $9$ to the ends are $0.59$ (left) and $0.61$ (right).
A symmetric window must fit inside $(8.41, 9.61)$, so it can reach only $0.59$.

blocks.html: "The δ." There is no single correct $\delta$: the definition asks for some $\delta$, and if one works, all smaller positive ones do too. A second slip is a $\delta$ that depends on $x$, like "$\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{|x + 2|}$": the window must be chosen before you look at individual points. Check a proposed $\delta$ by testing points near both ends of the window, on both sides of $a$.

blocks.html: Continuity at a point is the ε–δ limit with the hole filled in: the limit exists and equals the value. Writing the proofs teaches one trick you will use constantly, the "min with $1$," which restricts $x$ before bounding the rest of the expression.

$f$ is continuous at $a$ when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ with $|f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $|x - a| < \delta$. For $f(x) = x^{2}$: $|x^{2} - a^{2}| = |x - a|\,|x + a|$; if $|x - a| < 1$ then $|x + a| < 2|a| + 1$, so $\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1}\right)$ works.

The factor $|x - a|$ will be small; the trouble is the other factor $|x + a|$, which depends on $x$. Restricting $x$ to within $1$ of $a$ caps it: $$|x + a| = |(x - a) + 2a| \le |x - a| + 2|a| < 1 + 2|a|.$$ Now both conditions together, $|x - a| < 1$ and $|x - a| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1}$, give $$|x^{2} - a^{2}| < (2|a| + 1)\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1} = \varepsilon.$$ Taking $\delta$ to be the smaller of the two numbers guarantees both. The $1$ is arbitrary; any fixed positive number would do, with a different bound.

Proof, written out. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1}\right)$. Suppose $|x - a| < \delta$. Then $|x - a| < 1$, so $|x + a| < 2|a| + 1$, and $|x^{2} - a^{2}| = |x - a||x + a| < \delta(2|a| + 1) \le \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.cap: Continuity of $x^{2}$ at $a = 3$: set ε, then compare the recipe $\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{7}\right)$ with the largest δ the picture finds.

blocks.title: Running the recipe
blocks.q: Use $\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1}\right)$ for $x^{2}$ at $a = 3$ with $\varepsilon = 0.7$.
blocks.a: $\delta = 0.1$. (The largest δ is $\sqrt{9.7} - 3 \approx 0.1145$; the recipe is safe, not sharp.)

blocks.title: A different quadratic
blocks.q: For $f(x) = x^{2} - 4x$ at $a = 3$, write $|f(x) - f(3)|$ as a product and bound the second factor when $|x - 3| < 1$.

blocks.title: A cube
steps: On $(1, 3)$ the quadratic increases, so it stays below its value at $3$: $9 + 6 + 4 = 19$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the restriction. "$\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{5}$ works for $x^{2}$ at $2$" fails for large $\varepsilon$: with $\varepsilon = 100$ it allows $x = 21$, where $|x^{2} - 4| = 437$. The bound $|x + 2| < 5$ was only true for $|x - 2| < 1$, so $\delta$ must also be at most $1$. And never let δ depend on $x$; it is chosen once, from $\varepsilon$ and $a$.

blocks.html: Continuity can be tested with sequences instead of ε and δ, which turns everything you know about limits of sequences into facts about functions. The criterion is especially good at proving that a function is not continuous, where an ε–δ argument would be clumsy. It builds on ε–δ continuity.

Sequential criterion. $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and only if $f(x_n) \to f(a)$ for every sequence $x_n \to a$ (in the domain). So to prove a discontinuity, find one sequence $x_n \to a$ with $f(x_n) \not\to f(a)$, or two sequences giving different limits.

(Continuous implies the sequence condition.) Let $x_n \to a$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Take $\delta$ from continuity, then $N$ with $|x_n - a| < \delta$ for $n \ge N$; then $|f(x_n) - f(a)| < \varepsilon$. (Converse, by contrapositive.) If $f$ is not continuous at $a$, some $\varepsilon > 0$ has no working $\delta$. Try $\delta = \frac{1}{n}$: each fails, so there is an $x_n$ with $|x_n - a| < \frac{1}{n}$ but $|f(x_n) - f(a)| \ge \varepsilon$. Then $x_n \to a$ while $f(x_n) \not\to f(a)$. $\blacksquare$

The classic example is $f(x) = \sin\frac{1}{x}$ near $0$. Along $x_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2}$, $f(x_n) = 1$ for every $n$; along $x_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n}$, $f(x_n) = 0$. Both sequences tend to $0$, so no choice of $f(0)$ makes $f$ continuous there. Functions defined differently on rationals and irrationals work the same way, because every interval contains both kinds of numbers.

blocks.title: Choosing the sequence
blocks.q: For $f(x) = \cos\frac{1}{x}$ and $x_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/3}$, find $\lim f(x_n)$.
blocks.a: $\frac{1}{2}$. Another sequence gives $1$, so $\cos\frac{1}{x}$ has no limit at $0$.

blocks.title: Rational and irrational pieces
blocks.q: Let $f(x) = x^{2}$ for rational $x$ and $f(x) = x + 2$ for irrational $x$. Where is $f$ continuous?
steps: Near any $a$ there are rationals $r_n \to a$ and irrationals $t_n \to a$, giving $f(r_n) \to a^{2}$ and $f(t_n) \to a + 2$.
Continuity at $a$ needs $a^{2} = a + 2$, so $a = 2$ or $a = -1$. At those points every sequence gives the same limit, and $f$ is continuous; everywhere else it is not.

blocks.title: Thomae's function
blocks.q: Let $f\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = \frac{1}{q}$ for a fraction in lowest terms and $f(x) = 0$ for irrational $x$. Is $f$ continuous at $\frac{2}{3}$?
blocks.a: No. (At irrational points it is continuous: nearby rationals have large denominators.)

blocks.html: One good sequence proves nothing. "$f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \to f(0)$, so $f$ is continuous at $0$" is invalid: the criterion requires every sequence. One sequence can only prove a discontinuity. If you want to prove continuity, either handle an arbitrary sequence $x_n \to a$ or go back to ε and δ.

blocks.html: The intermediate value theorem from Calculus 1 looks obvious in a picture, but it is false over the rationals: $x^{2} - 2$ goes from negative to positive on $[1, 2]$ and is never $0$ at a rational point. Its proof needs completeness and continuity together.

Intermediate value theorem. If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) < y < f(b)$ (or $f(a) > y > f(b)$), then $f(c) = y$ for some $c \in (a, b)$. In particular a continuous function that changes sign on $[a, b]$ has a root there.

It is enough to handle $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$ (subtract $y$ otherwise). Let $c = \sup\{x \in [a, b] : f(x) < 0\}$, which exists by completeness. $f(c) < 0$ is impossible: by continuity $f$ would stay negative a little to the right of $c$, so $c$ would not be an upper bound (and $c \ne b$ since $f(b) > 0$). $f(c) > 0$ is impossible: $f$ would stay positive on an interval $(c - \delta, c]$, so $c - \delta$ would already be an upper bound, smaller than $c$ (and $c \ne a$ since $f(a) < 0$). So $f(c) = 0$. $\blacksquare$ A second proof halves the interval again and again, keeping the half where the sign changes; the nested intervals close in on a root. That proof is also an algorithm: bisection.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^{3} + 2x - 5$ changes sign on $[1, 2]$: trace the curve and see where it crosses.

blocks.title: Bisection by hand
blocks.q: For $f(x) = x^{3} + 2x - 5$ on $[1, 2]$ ($f(1) = -2 < 0 < 7 = f(2)$), run three bisection steps.
blocks.a: The root lies in $\left[\frac{5}{4}, \frac{11}{8}\right]$, an interval of length $\frac{1}{8}$.

blocks.title: Counting forced roots
blocks.q: A continuous $f$ has $f(-2) = 3$, $f(-1) = -1$, $f(0) = -4$, $f(1) = 2$, $f(2) = 5$. How many roots must it have in $[-2, 2]$?
steps: Sign changes: between $-2$ and $-1$, and between $0$ and $1$.

blocks.title: When the theorem does not apply
blocks.q: $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ has $f(-1) = -1 < 0 < 1 = f(1)$. Does the IVT give a root in $[-1, 1]$?
steps: $f$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$: it is not even defined at $0$.

blocks.html: Skipping the hypothesis, or reading too much into the conclusion. The function must be continuous on the whole closed interval; one bad point can let it jump over $0$. And the theorem only says a root exists, somewhere in $(a, b)$: it does not say there is only one, or where it is. For uniqueness you need more (for example, a strictly increasing function).

blocks.html: The extreme value theorem is the reason optimization problems on closed intervals always have answers. Its proof uses Bolzano–Weierstrass to catch a maximizing point, and every one of its hypotheses matters. It pairs with the intermediate value theorem: together they say a continuous function maps $[a, b]$ onto a closed interval $[m, M]$.

Extreme value theorem. A continuous function on a closed, bounded interval $[a, b]$ is bounded and attains a maximum and a minimum: there are $c, d \in [a, b]$ with $f(d) \le f(x) \le f(c)$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.

Bounded. If not, choose $x_n$ with $|f(x_n)| > n$. By Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence $x_{n_k} \to c$, and $c \in [a, b]$ because the interval is closed. By continuity $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(c)$, a finite number, contradicting $|f(x_{n_k})| > n_k$. Attained. Let $s = \sup f([a, b])$, finite now. Choose $x_n$ with $f(x_n) > s - \frac{1}{n}$. A subsequence converges to some $c \in [a, b]$, and $f(c) = \lim f(x_{n_k}) = s$. $\blacksquare$ Closed is used to keep $c$ in the interval, bounded to apply Bolzano–Weierstrass, and continuity to pass to the limit.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = 5 - (x - 1)^{2}$ on an interval: on a closed interval the top of the parabola is attained; remove an end and the supremum may be missed.

blocks.title: A closed interval
blocks.q: Find the maximum of $f(x) = x^{3} - 12x$ on $[-1, 4]$.
steps: $f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 12 = 0$ at $x = \pm 2$; only $x = 2$ is in the interval.

blocks.title: An open end
blocks.q: Find $\sup f$ on $(1, 3)$ for $f(x) = (x - 1)^{2}$, and decide whether it is attained.
steps: Every value is less than $4$, but values come as close to $4$ as you like.
blocks.a: $\sup f = 4$, not attained: no maximum. The interval is not closed.

blocks.title: Which hypothesis fails?
blocks.q: $f(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ on $[0, 2]$ takes values in $[0, 1)$ and has no maximum. Why does the EVT not apply?
steps: The interval is closed and bounded.
But $f$ jumps at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$: it is not continuous.

blocks.html: Using the theorem on the wrong set. On $(0, 1)$, $f(x) = x$ has supremum $1$ and no maximum; on $[0, \infty)$, it has no maximum at all; and $\frac{1}{x}$ (with $f(0) = 0$) on $[-1, 1]$ is not even bounded. When a problem asks whether a maximum exists, check all three: continuous, closed, bounded. When it does exist, find it among the critical points inside and the two ends.

blocks.html: In the proof that $x^{2}$ is continuous, the $\delta$ depended on the point $a$: the steeper the graph, the smaller $\delta$ had to be. Uniform continuity asks for one $\delta$ that works everywhere at once. On a closed, bounded interval it comes for free, by the same Bolzano–Weierstrass argument that proves the extreme value theorem, and it is the key to proving that continuous functions can be integrated.

$f$ is uniformly continuous on $S$ when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x, y \in S$ with $|x - y| < \delta$. Theorem: a continuous function on a closed, bounded interval is uniformly continuous. $\frac{1}{x}$ on $(0, 1)$ and $x^{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are continuous but not uniformly continuous.

Compare the quantifiers. Continuity: for every $a$ and every $\varepsilon$ there is a $\delta$ (which may depend on $a$). Uniform: for every $\varepsilon$ there is a $\delta$ that works for every $a$. For $\frac{1}{x}$ near $0$, the points $x = \delta$ and $y = \frac{\delta}{2}$ are within $\delta$, yet $\left|\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{y}\right| = \frac{1}{\delta}$, which is large: no single $\delta$ handles $\varepsilon = 1$. On $[a, b]$, a failure would produce pairs $x_n, y_n$ with $|x_n - y_n| \to 0$ but $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon$; Bolzano–Weierstrass gives subsequences converging to a common point $c$, and continuity at $c$ then forces $f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k}) \to 0$, a contradiction.

blocks.name: ra-epsdelta
blocks.cap: Uniform mode for $x^{2}$ on $[0, 3]$: drag the point along the interval. The purple strip shows the best δ at each point; the smallest of them is the one δ that works everywhere.

blocks.title: A line is the easy case
blocks.q: For $f(x) = \frac{3}{2}x + 7$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find the largest uniform $\delta$.
steps: $|f(x) - f(y)| = \frac{3}{2}|x - y|$, the same at every point.

blocks.title: The square on a closed interval
blocks.q: For $f(x) = x^{2}$ on $[0, 2]$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find the largest uniform $\delta$.
steps: For $y = x + t$ with $0 < t < \delta$: $y^{2} - x^{2} = t(2x + t)$, largest when $y = 2$: $t(4 - t)$.
As $t \to \delta$ this approaches $\delta(4 - \delta)$, so we need $\delta(4 - \delta) \le 0.1$, that is, $(2 - \delta)^{2} \ge 3.9$.
blocks.a: $\delta = 2 - \sqrt{3.9} \approx 0.0252$, set by the steep end of the interval.

blocks.title: Steep but still uniform
blocks.q: For $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0, \infty)$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, find the largest uniform $\delta$.
steps: $|\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}| \le \sqrt{|x - y|}$, with equality when one point is $0$.

blocks.html: Calling a point-dependent δ uniform. "$\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{2|a| + 1}$ works for $x^{2}$" is a perfectly good continuity proof at each $a$, but on $\mathbb{R}$ these $\delta$'s shrink to $0$ as $|a|$ grows, so no single one works. Ask: does my δ mention the point? If its smallest value over the set is $0$, the function is not uniformly continuous there.

blocks.html: In Calculus 1 the derivative was the limit of difference quotients, and the rules took over quickly. In analysis we go back to the definition, now with ε–δ limits behind it, because the interesting functions are exactly the ones the rules cannot handle: pieces glued together, or functions that oscillate near a point.

$f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$ when this limit exists (equivalently $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$). To use it: write the difference quotient, simplify it algebraically for $h \ne 0$, then take the limit, often with the squeeze theorem.

The difference quotient is the slope of the secant line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(a + h, f(a + h))$. As $h \to 0$ the secant turns into the tangent, and the derivative is its slope. Because the definition is a limit, every tool for limits applies: algebra to cancel the $h$, the squeeze theorem for oscillating factors, and one-sided limits at a corner.

blocks.name: secant
blocks.cap: The secant through $a$ and $a + h$ turns into the tangent as $h \to 0$.

blocks.title: A polynomial from scratch
blocks.q: For $f(x) = 2x^{2} + 3x$, simplify $\frac{f(1 + h) - f(1)}{h}$ and find $f'(1)$.

blocks.title: An oscillating function that is differentiable
blocks.q: Let $f(x) = x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x}$ for $x \ne 0$ and $f(0) = 0$. Find $f'(0)$.
steps: $\left|h\sin\frac{1}{h}\right| \le |h| \to 0$, so by the squeeze theorem the limit is $0$.
blocks.a: $f'(0) = 0$, even though $f'(x) = 2x\sin\frac{1}{x} - \cos\frac{1}{x}$ has no limit as $x \to 0$.

blocks.title: One power less, and it fails
blocks.q: Let $g(x) = x\sin\frac{1}{x}$ for $x \ne 0$ and $g(0) = 0$. Does $g'(0)$ exist?
steps: Along $h = \frac{1}{2\pi n}$ it is $0$; along $h = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2}$ it is $1$.
blocks.a: No limit, so $g'(0)$ does not exist (although $g$ is continuous at $0$).

blocks.html: Using the rules at a break point. For $f(x) = x^{2}$ ($x \le 1$) and $f(x) = 3x - 2$ ($x > 1$), "the derivative is $2x$ on the left and $3$ on the right" describes $f'$ away from $1$, but at $x = 1$ only the definition decides: the left quotient tends to $2$ and the right one to $3$, so $f'(1)$ does not exist. Likewise for $x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x}$: the formula for $f'(x)$ at $x \ne 0$ says nothing about $f'(0)$.

blocks.html: Differentiability is a stronger condition than continuity: a differentiable function is continuous, but a continuous function can have corners, as in Calculus 1. At a point where two formulas meet, the definition splits into one-sided limits.

Differentiable at $a$ implies continuous at $a$. At a break point, $f'(a)$ exists exactly when both one-sided limits of the difference quotient exist and agree. For pieces that meet at $c$, that means: the pieces agree at $c$ (continuity) and their slopes agree at $c$.

For $x \ne a$, $$f(x) - f(a) = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}\cdot(x - a).$$ As $x \to a$ the first factor tends to $f'(a)$ and the second to $0$, so by the product law $f(x) - f(a) \to f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0$: $f$ is continuous at $a$. $\blacksquare$ The converse fails: $|x|$ is continuous at $0$, but its quotient $\frac{|h|}{h}$ is $1$ for $h > 0$ and $-1$ for $h < 0$, so the one-sided limits disagree.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Gluing $x^{2}$ (for $x \le 1$) to a line: adjust $a$ and $b$ until the pieces meet and have the same slope. The answer is the tangent line $y = 2x - 1$.

blocks.html: A useful way to read differentiability: near $a$, the function is a line plus something much smaller than the distance to $a$. Precisely, $f(a + h) = f(a) + f'(a)h + r(h)$ with $\frac{r(h)}{h} \to 0$. A corner breaks this, because no single line fits the graph from both sides; a jump breaks it more badly, because no line through $(a, f(a))$ even comes close on one side. That is why every differentiable function is continuous, and why the converse must fail.

blocks.title: Making a function differentiable
blocks.q: Find $a$ and $b$ so that $f(x) = x^{2}$ for $x \le 2$ and $f(x) = ax + b$ for $x > 2$ is differentiable at $2$.
steps: The slopes must agree: the left derivative is $2x = 4$ at $x = 2$, the right one is $a$. So $a = 4$.
blocks.a: $a = 4$, $b = -4$: the line is the tangent line $y = 4x - 4$.

blocks.title: A corner, computed
blocks.q: For $f(x) = |x - 1|(x + 2)$, find the one-sided derivatives at $x = 1$.
steps: For $h > 0$ this tends to $3$; for $h < 0$ to $-3$.

blocks.html: Matching only one condition. For glued pieces, students often match the slopes and forget that the pieces must meet (then $f$ is not even continuous, so not differentiable), or check that the pieces meet and stop (then there may be a corner). Both equations are needed. And remember the logic: differentiable implies continuous; continuous does not imply differentiable.
